primary_secondary.note: Proposes and empirically validates the AI-Scrum framework with two teams.

study_type.claude: Case study (comparative case study using mixed methods)
study_type.note: Both describe the same design (comparative case study of two teams with survey, objective metrics and open-ended responses), but Claude classifies it as a case study and NotebookLM as mixed methods.

research_method.claude: Comparative case study with mixed methods: 5-point Likert surveys, objective metrics (time savings, defect rates, test coverage), benchmarking against traditional Scrum, open-ended responses; IBM SPSS v20 (Cronbach's alpha, correlations, regression, factor analysis)
research_method.nlm: Mixed methods: comparative case study with quantitative metrics, Likert-scale survey analysed in SPSS v20 and qualitative analysis; Cronbach's alpha, correlations, regression (R² = 0.63)
research_method.value: Comparative case study of two Scrum teams (professional vs. student) using the proposed AI-Scrum framework; mixed methods: 5-point Likert survey (19 respondents), objective metrics (time per Scrum phase in hrs/sprint, defect rates, test coverage), benchmarking against traditional Scrum, open-ended responses; IBM SPSS v20 (Cronbach's alpha, survey-metric correlations, regression R² = 0.63, factor analysis)
research_method.note: Factor analysis and benchmarking reported only by Claude (not contradicted).

context.claude: Mixed: professional team (6 members, dental scheduling system) and academic team (11 CS students, teacher attendance system), resource-constrained Libyan setting; n=19 survey respondents
context.nlm: Mixed: 1 professional team (6 members, dental scheduling system) and 1 academic team (11 CS students, teacher attendance system), resource-constrained Libya; 19 survey respondents
context.value: mixed; resource-constrained Libyan setting, one professional team (6 developers/Scrum Master, dental booking system) and one academic team (11 CS students, teacher attendance system); 19 survey respondents
context.note: Claude flags that Table II response rates (6/7 and 5/5) are inconsistent with 6 + 11 members and n=19.

dora_applied.note: Both state no productivity-measurement framework (DORA, SPACE, DevEx) is mentioned.

space_applied.note: Not mentioned by the paper according to both.

ai_discussed.note: AI tools (ClickUp AI, Windsurf, Diffblue Cover) embedded in every Scrum phase; AI impact on productivity is the core topic.

remote_covid.note: Work mode not reported by either.

data_window.note: Not stated by either (NotebookLM only mentions short-term sprint cycles).

cat_productivity.note: Time savings per Scrum phase (hrs/sprint, Table III) and sprint velocity.

cat_quality.note: Defect reduction (55–62%), test coverage (85–92%), code refactoring required.

cat_collaboration.note: No communication/review/coordination metric; stand-up duration is treated as efficiency/time savings by both, and AI trust is trust in tools, not team trust.

cat_satisfaction.note: Both label perceived productivity and AI trust/usability as 'Satisfaction', but under the definitions these are perceptual measures (cat_survey); no satisfaction or well-being measure in the full text.

cat_activity.note: Borderline: both label AI-generated code adoption (%) as Activity (NotebookLM also automated report adoption), but these are AI-adoption shares; no commit/PR/LOC counts.

cat_delivery.note: Both label sprint velocity as Delivery, but velocity is Productivity under the definitions; no deployment, lead-time or release metric ('faster delivery' only qualitative).

cat_devex.note: NotebookLM labels perceptual items 'Satisfaction / DevEx' but states the DevEx framework is not cited.

cat_agile.note: Time per Scrum ceremony/phase (backlog refinement, sprint planning, daily stand-ups) and sprint velocity in a Scrum process.

cat_survey.note: 5-point Likert survey (productivity perception, AI trust, challenges scales) plus open-ended responses.

evidence.quote: Validated through comparative case studies in professional and academic teams in resource constrained settings
Perceptual surveys : the number of respondents is 19 , and 5-point Likert scales was used
The study employed IBM SPSS v20 for statistical analysis, ensuring robust evaluation of the AI-Scrum framework.
Team 1 (Professionals): The team consistent of 6-members who developing a dental booking system.
Team 2 (Students): The team consistent of eleven students who building a teacher attendance system.
AI-Scrum as an architecture that strategically incorporates available AI tools into Agile processes in support of software engineering productivity.
Quantitative metrics which are:sprint velocity, defect rates and test coverage.
Academics saved 22% more time than professionals as shown in Table 3.
62% defect reduction (vs. 55% for academics), and 92% test coverage (Diffblue Cover).
Surveys: Feedback on an AI tool's usage with a Likert-scale on productivity, errors, and usability.
